Summary

Search risk at a glance

The short version

We tested 60 realistic customer queries against Reformation's search, live on site. The audit checks whether customers see a relevant top result, not just whether the search engine returns something.

This report focuses on the 30 queries where a customer likely hits a dead end: an off-topic result, a missing interpretation, a dropped constraint, or a relevant product buried too far down.

The first fix to ship: Boost exact product-type matches and brand signals over generic keyword scoring — This fixes Product Discovery by ensuring that when customers search for "sets," products with "Set" in the title rank above generic "Two Piece" items, and "sleep and loungewear" prioritizes actual sleepwear over basic tees.

Advanced Diagnostics

What the visible result set reveals

These checks stay inside the same query → results → audit boundary, but look beyond the single best result.

Result Set Purity

This checks how much of the visible result set is actually relevant, not just whether one good result exists somewhere. A noisy top 5 means customers must visually filter around weak results even when search technically found a match.

28%
top 5 relevant

Result

The visible result set is noisy: only 28% of top 5 results were relevant on average, and top 10 purity was 27%.

Evidence

  • "extended sizes": 0/5 relevant in top 5
  • "sleep and loungewear": 0/5 relevant in top 5
  • "clothing": 0/5 relevant in top 5
  • "sets": 0/5 relevant in top 5

How to remedy it

Tune ranking to demote low-relevance partial matches once a strong intent match exists. Add a top-N quality guardrail: for each important query class, require a minimum share of relevant results in the top 5, not only a good best-result position.

Top Result Trust

This asks whether the first result is defensible as the best thing to show a customer. A bad #1 is the clearest search failure because it shapes the shopper's first impression.

77%
questionable #1 results

Result

The first result is not reliable enough: 46 of 60 queries (77%) had a weak, partial, or clearly beaten #1 result.

Evidence

  • "outwear": #1 was "No results" (score 0.00). No visible result was available.
  • "newdresses": #1 was "No results" (score 0.00). No visible result was available.
  • "twopiecesets": #1 was "No results" (score 0.00). No visible result was available.
  • "summeredit": #1 was "No results" (score 0.00). No visible result was available.

How to remedy it

Add a stricter first-result threshold for high-intent queries. If the top result is weak and a stronger result exists lower, boost the stronger exact/category/brand match or suppress the weak partial match from rank #1.

Attribute Drift

This decomposes multi-attribute queries to see which terms survive into the top results. It distinguishes right-category-but-wrong-attribute failures from total search failures.

7
queries with attribute loss

Result

7 multi-attribute queries showed some attribute loss in the top 5. The audit separates preserved, partially preserved, and dropped terms so the team can see which part of the query is being lost.

Evidence

  • "show me linen": dropped show, me, linen; partially preserved none
  • "what's new this week": dropped what, this, week; partially preserved none
  • "back in stock items": dropped back, stock, item; partially preserved none
  • "silk dresses": dropped dresse; partially preserved none

How to remedy it

Extract query attributes before ranking and give required attributes explicit weight. For brand, size, material, activity, and style terms, penalize results that match the product type but omit or contradict the attribute.

Diversity vs Redundancy

This checks whether broad or exploratory queries show useful choice, or whether the top results are flooded by repeated variants. It is most useful for multi-brand or broad-catalog ecommerce, and less useful for true single-brand stores.

N/A
unique families in worst broad top 10

Result

Skipped because this diagnostic is mainly useful for multi-brand or broad-catalog ecommerce.

How to remedy it

Group color/size/variant duplicates under a product-family cap for broad queries. Keep exact product searches variant-rich, but diversify broad discovery queries across families, brands, styles, and use cases.

Recommendations

Prioritized Roadmap

1

Boost exact product-type matches and brand signals over generic keyword scoring

This fixes Product Discovery by ensuring that when customers search for "sets," products with "Set" in the title rank above generic "Two Piece" items, and "sleep and loungewear" prioritizes actual sleepwear over basic tees.

Critical Quick Win
2

Implement compound word splitting and common typo correction

This fixes Typo Tolerance by automatically handling merged words like "newdresses" → "new dresses" and common misspellings like "outwear" → "outerwear."

Critical Medium Effort
3

Add semantic understanding for subjective attributes and use cases

This fixes Shopping Context by mapping terms like "cute dresses" to casual styles rather than expensive cashmere, and "date night outfit" to appropriate dressy categories.

Critical Major Project
4

Configure natural language facet extraction

This fixes Filters & Constraints by recognizing phrases like "show me linen" as material filters and "what's new this week" as temporal constraints rather than literal keyword searches.

Critical Medium Effort
5

Add fashion abbreviation dictionary and synonym expansion

This fixes Brand & Model Search and Language Understanding by mapping "bf jeans" to "boyfriend jeans," "pjs" to pajamas, and "blouses" to tops/shirts.

Critical Quick Win
6

Implement result deduplication logic

This prevents the same product from appearing multiple times in search results, which currently wastes valuable result positions across multiple query types.

Moderate Quick Win
7

Add zero-results fallback with query suggestions

This provides helpful alternatives when searches like "date night outfit" or "outwear" return no results, guiding customers to successful searches.

Moderate Medium Effort
Industry Context

How You Compare

Metric Your Score Industry Target Source
Relevant result in top 3 31% 80%+ Baymard Institute
Average best result position #6 #1–2 Industry best practice
Irrelevant #1 result 47% <10% Industry best practice

70% of ecommerce sites cannot handle typos in their site search (Baymard Institute). Sites that do handle them gain a significant edge.

~30% of ecommerce visitors use site search, but they generate a disproportionate share of revenue — search users convert at 1.8–3x the rate of browse-only visitors (Econsultancy, Algolia).

31% of site searches end at a dead end — irrelevant results or zero results — across the average ecommerce site (Baymard Institute).

The top 3 results capture ~55–60% of all clicks. Results below position 3 are seen by a rapidly shrinking share of customers.

Revenue-Risk Failures

The queries most likely to cost sales

These examples show where the customer either sees no useful result, sees the wrong intent first, or has to dig past weaker results to find the right product.

#1 outwear No fuzzy matching

The search returned zero results — the customer reached a dead end.

Evidence

Query 'outwear' returned zero results despite being a common misspelling of 'outerwear'. The search engine failed to recognize this as a typo and provide any fuzzy matching or spell correction. The displacement metric shows the best result was at position #16, indicating relevant products exist in the catalog but weren't surfaced.

Fix

Add typo and fuzzy matching for high-value product, category, and brand terms so small spelling errors still reach the right products.

What the customer got

No results

An empty results page — nothing to click. The shopper hits a dead end and most leave.

#2 newdresses Zero results

The search returned zero results — the customer reached a dead end.

Evidence

Query 'newdresses' returned zero results despite being a merged compound word for 'new dresses' - a common product category. The search engine failed to split the compound word or perform any fuzzy matching to find relevant dress products.

Fix

Add query rewriting, token splitting, and fallback matching for this query pattern so customers do not hit a dead end.

What the customer got

No results

An empty results page — nothing to click. The shopper hits a dead end and most leave.

#3 twopiecesets Zero results

The search returned zero results — the customer reached a dead end.

Evidence

Query 'twopiecesets' returned zero results despite this being a merged compound word for 'two piece sets', a common product category. The search engine failed to recognize this as a compound word that should be split into 'two piece sets' to find relevant products.

Fix

Add query rewriting, token splitting, and fallback matching for this query pattern so customers do not hit a dead end.

#4 summeredit Zero results

The search returned zero results — the customer reached a dead end.

Evidence

Query 'summeredit' returned zero results despite the stats indicating a best result exists at position #16. The search engine completely failed to process this merged word query and returned no results to the customer.

Fix

Add query rewriting, token splitting, and fallback matching for this query pattern so customers do not hit a dead end.

#5 datenight No semantic understanding

The search returned zero results — the customer reached a dead end.

Evidence

Query 'datenight' returned zero results despite the analysis indicating a best result exists at position #16 with displacement of 15 positions. The search engine failed to recognize that 'datenight' is a compound word meaning 'date night' and should match products suitable for romantic evenings or special occasions.

Fix

Add synonym and semantic mappings for this customer phrasing so the engine recognizes the intended product need.

The search returned zero results — the customer reached a dead end.

The search engine failed to understand that 'date night outfit' is a use case query that should map to appropriate clothing items like dresses, blouses, or coordinated sets suitable for romantic occasions.

Fix

Add synonym and semantic mappings for this customer phrasing so the engine recognizes the intended product need.

Detailed Analysis

Product Discovery

5 examples
"sleep and loungewear"
Direct match · Critical · Best result at position #11

The search engine correctly retrieved sleep and loungewear products but ranked them terribly. The highest relevance sleep dresses (Aurora Sleep Dress at 0.535, Chloe Sleep Dress at 0.527, Poppy Sleep Dress at 0.523) were buried at positions #11, #4, and #7/#9 respectively. Meanwhile, completely irrelevant items dominated the top positions: Iris Knit Top appeared 4 times in the top 15 (positions #1, #3, #5, #14) with only 0.318 relevance, and basic tees (Rowan Crew Tee, Max Slim Tee) ranked #2 and #6 despite having the lowest relevance scores (0.297, 0.283).

Customer Saw

  1. Iris Knit Top (Kč 2,850.00)
  2. Rowan Crew Tee (Kč 1,400.00)
  3. Iris Knit Top (Kč 2,850.00)
  4. Chloe Sleep Dress (Kč 5,750.00)
  5. Iris Knit Top (Kč 2,850.00)

Should Have Seen

  1. Aurora Sleep Dress (Kč 4,900.00)
  2. Chloe Sleep Dress (Kč 5,750.00)
  3. Poppy Sleep Dress (Kč 4,900.00)

Best match was buried at position #11.

"clothing"

Meanwhile, lower-relevance items dominated the top: Espadrilles (0.451) at #1, Flat Sandals (0.400) at #2, and non-clothing items like Sunglasses (0.320) appeared at #8.

Positive Findings

What's Working

  • Retrieval is working — relevant results were found in 22 of 60 queries. The primary issue is ranking, not finding: the right results exist in the result set but aren't being surfaced at the top.
  • Close to correct on 16 queries ("new dresses", "extended sizes", "dreses"): the best result was within the top 3, just not at #1.

Scope and Boundaries

What this audit covers

Included

Search relevance, ranking quality, retrieval gaps, query interpretation failures, visible result ordering, and prioritized fixes based on the tested query set.

Not included

Implementation work, platform configuration changes, merchandising strategy, analytics instrumentation, or a full conversion-rate analysis beyond the search result experience.

Next Steps

We'd welcome the opportunity to walk you through these findings in detail and discuss a remediation plan tailored to your team's priorities and timeline.

The issues identified in this audit are fixable — most ecommerce search platforms support the capabilities tested here, and the roadmap above is ordered by impact to help you prioritize.
